stops.name: The muddy waters of Baljuna, covenant of the nineteen
stops.campa: Toghrul's son Senggüm, fearing the marriage alliance Temüjin proposes between their two households, turns his father against his adopted son; ambushed twice, Temüjin is routed at the Qalaqaljid Sands and flees north with only a handful of followers. At a muddy pool called Baljuna, nineteen companions of six different peoples and three faiths, Nestorian Christian, Muslim, and shaman, find nothing to drink but the churned water itself, share it out in cupped hands, and swear to stand by one another through whatever comes, victory or ruin. Their descendants, the Baljunatu, will be seated near the throne for generations for that single cup of mud.

stops.name: Jeje'er Heights, the fall of the Kereit and the death of Toghrul
stops.campa: Revived by the Baljuna oath, Temüjin gathers a fresh army in secret and falls without warning on Toghrul's unready camp at the Jeje'er Heights on the lower Kherlen, breaking the Kereit khanate after three days of hard fighting. Toghrul and Senggüm flee west with almost no one; the old khan who once called Yesügei anda and took in his son as a ward is caught alone at the Naiman border and killed by a suspicious guard who does not recognize the beggarly rider before him, his severed head brought to the Naiman court on a felt some days later.

stops.name: Chakirmaut, foot of Mount Naqu: the Naiman broken, the seal-keeper found
stops.campa: The last confederation able to contest the steppe, the Naiman of Tayang Khan, gather Merkit and Taichiud remnants and Jamukha himself at the foot of Mount Naqu in the Khangai. Warned that Tayang Khan has scorned these upstart Mongols as men who smell of smoke and sour milk, Temüjin destroys the coalition in days of running battle. Among the captured is Tata-tonga, a Uyghur scribe found still guarding the Naiman treasury and its golden seal; asked its purpose, he explains the stamp of authority pressed in wax, and Temüjin keeps him at court to teach the seal, and soon the alphabet behind it, to his own sons.

stops.name: The last meeting, the death of Jamukha
stops.campa: Hunted down at last by his own five remaining generals, who bind him with his own belt rather than kill him themselves and bring him before his anda, a loyalty Temüjin punishes rather than rewards, since men who betray their own lord for any cause cannot be kept near him, Jamukha is offered his life and the brotherhood renewed. He refuses: one mountain, he says, cannot shelter two tigers, and asks only to die without his blood spilled on the ground, that his soul rest quiet among his own bones. Temüjin grants it; Jamukha is broken-limbed and strangled in the manner reserved for nobles, and buried with honor.

stops.name: The source of the Onon: proclaimed Chinggis Khan
stops.campa: With every rival broken, the peoples of the felt-walled tents gather by the hundred thousand at the headwaters of the Onon, encampments spreading for miles across the grass. A standard of nine white yak-tails is raised, and the shaman Kököchü, called Teb Tenggeri, spokesman of Heaven, declares that every gur-khan of the earth's lands is now subdued and that by Heaven's own decree Temüjin's title shall be Chinggis Khan. The scattered clans, Merkit, Naiman, Kereit, Tatar, Taichiud, and his own Borjigin, cease to be tribes and become instead a single Yeke Mongghol Ulus, the Great Mongol Nation, its men reorganized into thousands under captains who answer to him alone.

stops.name: Avarga on the Kherlen, the yam strung across the steppe
stops.campa: From his new ordu on the Kherlen, Chinggis Khan orders relay stations built a day's ride apart across the whole breadth of the nation, each stocked with fresh horses, food, and a keeper bound to serve any rider carrying his tablet of authority. A message that once took a season now crosses the steppe in days; envoys, merchants, and tribute travel under the same guarantee of safe passage, and the roads of Asia become, for the first time anyone can remember, places where a lone traveler might cross an empire and come to no harm.

stops.name: Avarga on the Kherlen, the law and the letters
stops.campa: The khan sets Tata-tonga, the captured Uyghur scribe, to bend the Old Uyghur alphabet to the sounds of Mongol speech and teach it to the princes and the new chancellery, the first script the steppe has ever owned as its own. In the same years the customary law of the tribes on theft, on the sharing of plunder, on never abandoning a companion in battle, is gathered and set down as the Great Yassa, binding khan and herder under the same words, though no complete copy of it will outlive the empire that kept it.

stops.name: The mountain above the Kherlen, three days of prayer before the Jin war
stops.campa: Before striking the empire that once nailed his ancestor Ambaghai Khan to a wooden mule and armed the Tatars against his people, Chinggis Khan climbs alone to a hill above his camp, bares his head, unbelts his coat, and lies before the Eternal Blue Sky reciting three generations of Jin wrongs while his whole nation waits below, bareheaded and fasting. On the fourth dawn he comes down with his answer: Heaven has promised victory and vengeance. That spring the tümens cross the Gobi and break the Jin field army at the Yehuling pass.
stops.quote: The Eternal Blue Sky has promised us victory and vengeance.
stops.quote_source: The verdict announced on the fourth dawn before the Jin war, 1211, as given in Weatherford, Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World

stops.name: Zhongdu, the Jin capital starved into surrender
stops.campa: When the Jin emperor abandons Zhongdu for the safer south at Kaifeng, Chinggis Khan reads the flight as bad faith and fresh cause for war. The Mongols close a siege that runs the whole winter through; granaries fail, the starving are reduced to eating one another, and in June the city that will one day be Beijing falls and burns for a month, its palaces stripped and put to the torch. The Jin, once suzerain of half of China, are broken down to a rump state clinging to the south bank of the Yellow River.

stops.name: The road to Otrar: merchants sent, merchants slaughtered
stops.campa: Hoping for trade rather than war with the new Muslim power beyond the Tien Shan, Chinggis Khan sends word to Sultan Muhammad of Khwarezm proposing only friendship and open roads, and follows it with a caravan of some four hundred fifty merchants under his own seal. At Otrar the governor Inalchuq, a kinsman of the Sultan, seizes the whole company as spies and puts every one of them but a single camel-driver to death, the lone survivor who crosses the desert alone to bring the khan the news that will end an empire.
stops.quote: I am master of the lands of the rising sun, while you rule those of the setting sun. Let us conclude a firm treaty of friendship and peace.
stops.quote_source: Reported by Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani and later Persian chroniclers of the embassy of 1218

stops.name: Otrar, molten silver for the governor's eyes
stops.campa: A second embassy demanding Inalchuq's surrender is answered with the beheading of the Muslim envoy and the shaving of his two Mongol companions' beards, an insult worse than the first killing. Chinggis Khan gathers every tümen and marches in person, dividing his sons among the empire's cities while he himself besieges Otrar; the town falls after months of siege, and Inalchuq, taken alive, is said to have molten silver poured into his eyes and ears until he dies, punishment measured exactly to the crime of greed that started the whole war.

stops.name: Bukhara, the punishment of God in the Friday mosque
stops.campa: Bukhara's garrison is cut down at the river crossing; the citadel holds twelve days more before it too falls. Chinggis Khan rides his horse into the courtyard of the great Friday mosque, mistaking its tall minaret for a palace, and has the city's notables brought before him. Speaking through an interpreter, he tells the gathered crowd that their own great sins have brought this ruin upon them, and that he himself is only the instrument of it. The city burns; only the slender Kalyan minaret is spared, said to have made even the khan bow his head to look up at it.
stops.quote: I am the punishment of God. If you had not committed great sins, God would not have sent a punishment like me upon you.
stops.quote_source: Ata-Malik Juvaini, Tarikh-i Jahangushay (The History of the World Conqueror), on the fall of Bukhara, 1220
